latin: Subiectum et propria passio realiter distinguuntur.
translation: A subject and its proper attribute are really distinct.
translation_note: 'propria passio' is a scholastic technical term for a property that, while not part of a thing's essential definition, belongs to it inseparably and exists only in that subject (the standard example being 'snubness' in a nose), per Farmer's note (farmer1998:11682).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-swarm-batch4, from Latin at farmer1998:11650

sources.text: Thomas Aquinas, Commentaria in octo libros Physicorum Aristotelis, Book 7, Lect. 5
sources.pico_relation: Edelheit locates the thesis's doctrine here, in Thomas's discussion of a secondary kind of change (alteration)

sources.text: Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae I, q. 11, a. 1: 'unum enim nihil aliud significat quam ens indivisum'
sources.pico_relation: further Thomistic parallel Edelheit quotes alongside the thesis, on 'one' adding only the negation of division to being

doctrine: The thesis states that a subject and its proper attribute are distinguished in reality, not merely in thought (farmer1998:11650). Edelheit finds it in Thomas's commentary on Aristotle's Physics, Book 7, Lecture 5, in a discussion of secondary change (edelheit2022:11635), and links it to Thomas's Summa theologiae I, q. 11, a. 1, where 'unum' is said to add to being only the negation of division (edelheit2022:11662). Farmer's note states that the thesis begins a complex series on the substance/accident distinction, and that on metaphysical grounds Pico elsewhere rejected all distinctions between 'separable' and 'inseparable' accidents (farmer1998:11682).
context: Edelheit finds an analogy in William of Ockham linking theses 23 and 24: Ockham holds that 'being' and 'one' relate to each other just as, generally, 'quality' (passio) relates to 'subject' (subiectum) (edelheit2022:11733). Edelheit suggests Pico may have had this analogy in mind while composing theses 23-24, but leaves the question open: 'One can only wonder whether Pico had this analogy of William at the back of his mind while working of [sic] theses 23 and 24' (edelheit2022:11733; edelheit2022:11739).
historiography: Edelheit is the only scholar in the sources consulted to discuss this thesis; he treats it as part of a network of theses (23-25, 27) on the being/one and substance/accident problems drawn from Thomas and, possibly, Ockham (edelheit2022:11733; edelheit2022:11870).

quotations.text: One can only wonder whether Pico had this analogy of William at the back of his mind while working of [sic] theses 23 and 24.

not_established: Whether Pico in fact drew on Ockham for this thesis, as opposed to Thomas alone: Edelheit leaves this an open question (edelheit2022:11739).
Any reception of this thesis by the 1487 commission or in the Apologia: not established by the sources consulted.
